text:
The University of Cambridge is a historic collegiate research university located in Cambridge, England, with a founding date of 1209. It is organized into 31 self-governing colleges and over 150 departments and schools, covering a wide range of academic disciplines. The university operates on a distinctive academic year divided into three terms: Michaelmas (October–December), Lent (January–March), and Easter (April–June). Undergraduate teaching takes place during eight-week "full terms," during which all students are required to live within three miles of the Church of St Mary the Great, a tradition known as "keeping term." A hallmark of Cambridge education is the supervisory system, where students typically meet weekly with a tutor or doctoral student for small-group discussions on assigned work, a pedagogical method often cited as unique to Cambridge and Oxford.
Cambridge boasts a prestigious reputation and ranks highly in global university rankings. Its academic profile includes renowned research departments, extensive libraries, and numerous museums, such as the Fitzwilliam Museum and the Museum of Archaeology and Anthropology. The university is a member of the Russell Group and the League of European Research Universities. Historically, it has produced numerous Nobel laureates, including Isaac Newton, Charles Darwin, and Stephen Hawking, and has educated prominent figures in politics, literature, and science. While the university has faced criticism regarding admissions processes and historical issues, it maintains strong ties with the high-tech cluster known as Silicon Fen and continues to expand its facilities and research capabilities.
